messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 48
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Fashion Designer
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 34

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Somatic (Nausea): Feeling nauseous, Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings, Checking Locks: repeatedly check locks, doors, or windows, Busyness: I work hard at keeping busy with other things
  Threat: Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Samir is a 48-year-old fashion designer who came to therapy after a series of nights he could no longer outrun. The event that changed everything happened three years ago, at the downtown studio where he was overseeing final alterations for a runway collection. A short circuit ignited stored bolts of silk and chiffon; the fire spread so fast that by the time Samir smelled smoke, the main exit was already blocked. He managed to crawl through a side door, his hands blistering from a door handle that had turned to iron, his throat raw from the chemical tang of melting synthetics. For years afterward, that taste would rise in his mouth without warning—bitter and acrid, impossible to swallow away. The memory never arrived whole. Instead, Samir would be sketching a new hemline or driving home from a client meeting, and suddenly he would feel the searing heat on his skin, a precise temperature that belonged only to that door handle, and his stomach would turn violently, leaving him pale and hunched over the nearest sink. The taste would come next, and then the fragments—screams from the other end of the hall, the pop of ceiling tiles, the weight of a body against his back as someone pushed past. It never felt like remembering. It felt like it was happening right then, the sweat breaking out on his forehead, his hands searching for something cool to press against his face.

In the months that followed, Samir’s life contracted. He kept himself moving constantly—12-hour days at the studio, then freelance projects in the evenings, then gym sessions at midnight—because stillness was where the taste returned and the heat crawled up his arms. If he stopped, the fragments would come; if he kept working, he could drown them in fabric swatches and seam allowances. But busyness had a price. His concentration frayed. He would stare at a pattern draft for twenty minutes, the lines blurring as his eyes went elsewhere—checking the studio’s vents, searching for smoke, calculating how fast he could reach the fire escape. Every new location required a mental map of exits before he could breathe. Restaurants, theaters, even a friend’s living room: Samir would scan the room for hazards, the way a designer scans a mannequin for flaws. He had started checking the locks on his apartment door three, four, five times before he could sleep, and then he would lie awake, running escape routes through his head until dawn.

There were nights when the pressure built to a point he could not think his way out of. Then Samir would lock the bathroom door and press the edge of a scissors blade against his forearm—just hard enough to break skin, just deep enough to turn the taste of smoke into something cleaner, more immediate. The pain grounded him, pulled him out of the hot, sick fog of the memory and back into the cold tile floor. He had told no one. His divorce had already happened before the fire, his ex-wife citing the long hours and the way he had grown distant, but he knew this was something else. He had become a man who checked every window twice, who could not focus on a conversation because he was watching the ceiling for sprinklers, who sometimes had to excuse himself from a fitting when a client’s perfume reminded him of paraffin and ash.

What finally brought Samir to the clinic was a Tuesday morning in his studio. A new intern had brought in a space heater, and the moment the heating element clicked on, Samir smelled it—that same chemical warmth—and he vomited onto a half-finished gown. He stood there, shaking, the fragments swarming, the taste thick on his tongue, and he knew he could not design his way out of this one. He made the appointment with the number his primary care doctor had given him months ago. He is afraid that if he slows down enough to talk about the fire, he will be pulled back into it permanently, trapped in that hot, choking moment forever. But he is also tired—tired of mapping every room, tired of the nightly checks, tired of the taste that never quite leaves his mouth. He wants to feel like the man who used to sketch without looking over his shoulder. He wants to walk into a room and see the clothes, not the exits.
